claims.text: The initial alloy is a metastable, single-phase solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
Demanding mechanical loading creates local stress concentrations in the alloy.
Local stress concentration promotes kinetically activated decomposition and stress-induced segregation at grain boundaries.
Stress-induced grain-boundary segregation causes brittle intermetallic precipitates to nucleate.
High stress and low temperature cause local compositional fluctuations in the initially uniform solid solution.
Stress concentration at grain boundaries locally enhances atomic mobility.
Grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes toughness loss and promotes brittle fracture.
Relative to the baseline, mechanically loaded samples tested at low temperature will have lower Charpy impact energy or fracture toughness.
Mechanically loaded, low-temperature samples will show brittle precipitates at grain boundaries by electron microscopy.
Unloaded or mildly loaded samples maintained at ambient temperature preserve a uniform single-phase structure without brittle secondary phases.
The ambient-temperature baseline has higher toughness than the intensely loaded, low-temperature condition.
The proposed effect is significant when intense high-strain-rate or cyclic loading is combined with low temperature.
At ambient temperature or very low stress, the original single-phase structure and high toughness are maintained.
The stress and temperature thresholds for segregation and the precipitation rate vary with alloy composition.
Oxidation and pre-existing microstructural heterogeneities may independently influence the fracture outcome.
